strengths: The proposed detector is simple and potentially useful: quantizing proxy-LM surprisals and comparing first-order transition matrices to fixed human/machine references gives a cheap one-pass online scoring procedure after reference construction.

The empirical section is broad in scope, covering multiple datasets, open- and closed-source generators, proxy-model variation, reference/test length ablations, non-English settings, paraphrasing, throughput, and a comparison to R-Detect.

The paper makes a serious attempt to connect the statistic to likelihood-free/reference-based testing and to explain the choice of the number of bins through a bias-variance tradeoff, which is a promising direction for making such detectors less heuristic.

Results are often strong, especially against closed-source models and in settings where the machine reference is source-matched, suggesting that surprisal-transition dynamics may contain a robust detection signal.
weaknesses: The main experimental setup appears to give SurpMark source- and domain-matched machine references generated by the same model used for the test machine texts, while most baselines are zero-shot/statistic-based methods without access to such reference data. This makes the comparison potentially unfair and weakens the black-box deployment claim: the method seems to assume the detector can obtain representative machine samples from the unknown or target generator.

The central practical claim that fixed references can be reused is not fully supported under realistic shifts. The paper samples 300 human texts per dataset and generates paired machine references per source model, then tests on the same dataset/source construction. It does not convincingly evaluate mismatched domains, unseen generators without source-specific references, or mixed/unknown generator populations.

The theoretical development has notable issues and ambiguities. The appendix treats GJS as an f-divergence but appears to conflate the skew weight w=alpha/(1+alpha) with alpha itself, leading to expressions such as alpha t + 1 - alpha even though alpha=N/n can exceed 1. The asymptotic variance notation is also inconsistent, alternating between long-run variances and variances of sums with scaling by N^2/n^2, making the normality theorem hard to verify.

The discretization analysis depends on strong assumptions that are not empirically checked or clearly justified for surprisal sequences, including ergodic first-order Markov dynamics, bounded mixing/hitting time O(1), and pi_min proportional to 1/k. These assumptions are central to the claimed k*=Theta(N^1/5) rule but may not hold in the proposed application.

Several presentation and reliability issues undermine confidence. For example, Table 1 contains apparent arithmetic errors in averaged AUROC values, and some formulas/proofs contain typographical or indexing mistakes. These are not merely cosmetic in a paper that relies heavily on quantitative comparisons and theory.

Reproducibility is inadequate despite the claim that experiments are reproducible. The paper does not provide code, seeds, exact prompts, decoding parameters for generated text, details of train/test splits, baseline implementation settings, or how thresholds/hyperparameters are selected beyond coarse descriptions.

The ethics discussion is very brief for a detector paper. It does not seriously address false-positive harms, domain/language bias, adversarial adaptation, use in high-stakes academic or employment settings, or how users should interpret uncertain scores.

strengths: The manuscript addresses an important and timely problem: efficient black-box detection of LLM-generated text without per-input regeneration.
The proposed reference-based surprisal-transition idea is coherent and potentially useful as a lightweight detector, especially if reference corpora can be reused at scale.

The paper reports broad-looking empirical comparisons across several datasets, source models, proxy models, text lengths, and non-English settings, and includes some ablations on bin count and reference/test length.
weaknesses: The theoretical support is not convincing. The analysis relies on strong, unvalidated assumptions such as first-order ergodic Markov surprisal dynamics, bounded mixing/hitting time, and pi_min scaling; the appendix proofs also contain questionable steps, loose reductions, and unclear notation around the asymptotic-normality result.

The empirical protocol does not justify the broad robustness and deployment claims. Reference and test data appear to come from closely matched dataset/source-model settings, with machine texts generated from the first 30 tokens of paired human texts, which may make the task easier than realistic open-world detection.

The evaluation is incomplete for a detector. AUROC averages dominate the evidence, while false-positive behavior, threshold transfer, calibration, confidence intervals, low-base-rate deployment behavior, and stronger robustness benchmarks are not adequately examined.

The ablations do not isolate the actual contribution well enough. Simpler alternatives such as binned surprisal histograms, non-Markov summaries, other divergences, cross-domain references, smoothing choices, and reference mismatch conditions are not sufficiently tested.

Reproducibility is weak despite the reproducibility statement. Exact prompts, decoding parameters, splits, seeds, threshold-selection rules, closed-source model settings, and baseline implementation details are not specified enough for reliable replication.
The ethics and limitations discussion is too shallow for AI-text detection, especially given risks of false accusations, domain/language bias, adaptive evasion, and misuse in high-stakes settings.

strengths: The paper proposes a simple and useful black-box detector, SurpMark, that avoids per-instance regeneration by summarizing token surprisal dynamics with discretized first-order transition matrices and comparing test passages to fixed human/machine references via a generalized Jensen-Shannon gap.

The empirical evaluation is broad: results cover multiple datasets, 9 open-source and 3 closed-source generators, several proxy LMs, non-English settings, paraphrasing attacks, throughput, reference size, test length, and comparisons against many strong statistics-based baselines. The reported AUROC gains and throughput advantages are practically meaningful.

The method is computationally attractive. Building references once and using a single proxy-model pass at test time is a compelling design point relative to DetectGPT-style regeneration methods, especially for high-throughput deployment.

The paper attempts to connect the detector to likelihood-free hypothesis testing, gives a discretization bias-variance analysis, and empirically checks score normality. Even if some assumptions are strong, this theoretical framing is valuable and more informative than a purely heuristic detector.
The presentation of the main method is mostly clear, and the ablations on bins, reference length, test length, and proxy choice help explain when the method works best.
weaknesses: The central theoretical claims are stronger than the analysis appears to support. The discretization result relies on existence of a good partition, but the implemented quantizer is k-means on pooled surprisals; the paper does not prove that this practical choice satisfies the bound. Similarly, the first-order Markov, ergodicity, bounded mixing, and pi_min assumptions are strong and not empirically validated for real surprisal sequences.

The claimed exact identification of the GJS gap with a normalized log-likelihood ratio seems to ignore or under-specify details such as initial-state probabilities, concatenation boundary transitions, and stationary constraints. The asymptotic-normality statement also has scaling/notation ambiguities around whether the variance terms are for sums or normalized averages, making the theorem hard to verify as stated.

The black-box setting is somewhat weakened by the need for machine reference corpora. In the main experiments, the machine references appear to be generated from the same source model being detected. This is useful but does not fully test the common deployment case where the generator family is unknown, mixed, or unavailable for reference generation.

Reproducibility is incomplete. The paper gives datasets, model lists, hardware, and broad sample sizes, but it does not provide code, seeds, exact prompts, decoding parameters, preprocessing choices, threshold selection details, or precise instructions for reproducing the generated corpora and baselines. The reproducibility statement is too brief.

The evaluation is convincing on AUROC, but more deployment-oriented calibration analysis is needed: false-positive rates at low FPR, threshold transfer across domains/models, robustness to human editing, mixed human-AI text, and adversarial paraphrases stronger than T5 would be important for the claimed real-world suitability.

Limitations and ethics are underdeveloped. The ethics statement does not seriously discuss harms from false accusations, surveillance use, demographic/domain bias in human references, or appropriate uncertainty reporting. There is no explicit limitations section, despite clear constraints around reference availability, text length, and distribution shift.

The writing is generally understandable but has several presentation issues: some tables are cramped, a few formulas/appendix references appear inconsistent, and the main text sometimes overclaims robustness or theoretical principledness relative to the evidence provided.

strengths: SurpMark is a simple and computationally attractive detector: it uses one proxy-LM pass, fixed human/machine references, discretized surprisal transitions, and a GJS proximity score, avoiding per-input perturbation or regeneration used by several baselines.

The empirical evaluation is unusually broad, covering many open- and closed-source generators, multiple datasets, non-English settings, mixed-domain/mixed-generator cases, OOD reference shifts, paraphrase and prompt-engineered attacks, low-FPR TPR, proxy-model sensitivity, and throughput.

The core empirical signal is plausible and well motivated: modeling first-order dynamics of surprisal states improves over unigram surprisal-state distributions, especially for stronger closed-source models where marginal surprisal gaps are small.
The paper includes useful ablations on bin count, quantization schemes, Markov order, distance metric, test/reference length, and threshold selection, which helps characterize when the method works.
The impact statement is appropriately cautious that detector outputs should not be used as definitive evidence in high-stakes settings.
weaknesses: The practical black-box framing is somewhat overstated. The main setup builds machine references from the same source-model family and similar prompting/data distribution as the test setting; in real deployments the generator and prompting process may be unknown. Mixed-generator and OOD experiments help, but do not fully resolve this dependency on representative machine references.

The theoretical contribution appears weaker than claimed. The discretization and Markov analyses rely on strong idealized assumptions such as ergodicity, bounded mixing, stationary first-order kernels, pi_min scaling, and smoothness of continuous transition kernels, and the connection from these results to the actual k-means quantizer and finite text passages is indirect.

Some proof details are not fully convincing or are under-specified, e.g. the O(1/k) discretization argument invokes existence of partitions from prior f-divergence quantization results but the algorithm uses k-means; the row-wise Markov f-divergence weighting and empirical stationary distributions are handled informally; and constants/log factors make the N^{1/5} bin guidance more qualitative than operational.

Reproducibility is incomplete: I did not find a code or artifact release, exact random seeds, full prompts for all generation/attack settings, or detailed baseline implementation settings sufficient to reproduce the many tables. Closed-source model defaults may also change over time.

The experimental protocol may involve substantial implicit tuning. Results are often reported for k=6/7/8, figures use k-optimized curves, and the paper does not clearly separate validation from test selection for hyperparameters and threshold analyses.

Several presentation issues reduce confidence: some table averages appear inconsistent or typo-prone, there are grammar/formatting errors, and the manuscript is very long with many appendix claims that are hard to audit. The central claims would be stronger with tighter reporting and a clearer reproducibility package.

strengths: The paper studies an important problem: black-box detection of LLM-generated text under proxy-model mismatch and deployment cost constraints.

SurpMark is simple and potentially useful: it scores text with one proxy-LM pass, discretizes token surprisals, models first-order transition dynamics, and compares to human/machine reference transition matrices via a GJS-based statistic.

The empirical section is broad in surface coverage, including many generators, datasets, languages, test lengths, decoding settings, paraphrasing, perturbations, and mixed-domain/mixed-generator scenarios.
The paper includes ablations for binning, Markov order, reference size, test length, distance metric, and proxy model choice, which helps clarify which ingredients are doing some work.
The impact statement appropriately notes that AI-text detection is probabilistic and should not be used alone for high-stakes decisions.
weaknesses: The main experimental protocol appears to give SurpMark privileged information. For each evaluated source model, the machine reference corpus is generated from that same source model, including closed-source systems. This substantially weakens the claimed black-box/unknown-generator setting and makes comparisons to baselines unfair, since most baselines are not given target-generator reference samples.

The central claims about robustness and deployment are therefore not fully supported. The method may work well when one has matched human and machine reference corpora, but the paper repeatedly frames the problem as unknown-source black-box detection. The evaluation does not convincingly establish performance when the machine reference is unavailable, stale, generated by different prompts, or mismatched to the true deployment distribution.

The theory has limited relevance to the empirical claims. It analyzes an idealized first-order Markov process over discretized proxy-surprisal states under strong ergodicity/mixing and occupancy assumptions. These assumptions are not validated in a way that would support the strong real-world detection claims, and the derived bin scaling is later tuned with empirical grid search rather than used as a genuinely predictive design rule.

There are internal inconsistencies in the score/hypothesis interpretation. The definition ΔGJS = GJS(machine,test) - GJS(human,test) implies negative scores are more machine-like, but parts of the appendix describe the sign in the opposite direction; the H0/H1 labels also appear reversed in the normality table. These mistakes raise concerns about care in the statistical presentation and thresholding discussion.

Hyperparameter and threshold selection are not cleanly separated from evaluation. The paper reports multiple k values, calibrates the scaling constant empirically, and discusses oracle-like threshold sweeps, but does not clearly define a deployment-valid validation protocol for choosing k, references, and thresholds without test-set feedback.

Several reported robustness results are surprisingly strong, sometimes near-perfect under paraphrasing or perturbation, but the setup may preserve artifacts from paired construction, matched references, or source/domain leakage. More stringent adversarial and naturally occurring OOD settings are needed before accepting the robustness claims.

The baselines may not be budget- or information-matched. SurpMark uses offline target-like machine references while baselines are mostly zero-shot or per-input methods; the paper emphasizes lower per-test regeneration cost but does not adequately account for the cost and feasibility of collecting matched machine references for each source/domain.

Reproducibility is incomplete. The manuscript gives high-level implementation details and hardware, but lacks sufficient detail on prompts, exact dataset splits, API versions, random seeds, preprocessing, baseline implementations, and code/data release plans. Closed-source model results in particular may be hard to reproduce.

The limitations and ethics discussion is too shallow for this application. The paper notes false-positive risks but does not evaluate demographic, linguistic, domain, non-native-speaker, or high-stakes false accusation harms, despite positioning the method as suitable for real-world deployment.

strengths: The paper proposes a simple and useful detector: tokenize with a proxy LM, quantize token surprisals, summarize first-order transition dynamics, and classify by a generalized Jensen-Shannon gap to fixed human/machine references. This is computationally attractive because it avoids per-input perturbation or regeneration and amortizes reference construction.

The empirical evaluation is broad and generally convincing. The paper compares against many strong statistics-based baselines across open-source and closed-source generators, multiple domains, non-English datasets, mixed-domain and mixed-generator settings, OOD reference shifts, paraphrasing, prompt-engineered attacks, low-FPR TPR, proxy-model variation, and throughput. The results consistently show SurpMark matching or exceeding baselines, especially for closed-source generators where marginal likelihood signals are weak.

The method is well motivated by an interpretable observation about surprisal transition dynamics, and the ablations support the main design choices: first-order transitions outperform unigram surprisal-state distributions, GJS outperforms L1/L2 in the reported setting, k-means binning is usually stronger than equal-width/equal-mass binning, and higher-order Markov models suffer from sparsity.

The theoretical analysis is useful as design guidance rather than just decoration. It clarifies the discretization-estimation tradeoff, motivates the k = Theta(N^(1/5)) scaling, and connects the GJS statistic to a likelihood-ratio style relative test under an idealized discretized Markov model.

The paper includes an appropriate impact statement warning that detector outputs should not be treated as definitive evidence in high-stakes settings, and it discusses some limitations such as the first-order Markov approximation and possible pretraining exposure effects on human text.
weaknesses: The central robustness claim is somewhat stronger than the evidence warrants. In the main experiments, machine references appear to be generated with the same source model and prompting procedure as the test machine samples, which is easier than deployment against unknown or evolving generators. The mixed-generator and cross-reference experiments help, but the practical requirement of maintaining representative machine references deserves a more explicit treatment.

Reproducibility is only partially addressed. The manuscript gives many implementation details, model lists, hardware, decoding settings, and algorithms, but I did not find a clear code/data release statement, random seeds, exact prompts for all generation/adversarial settings, or enough detail to reproduce closed-source API outputs. Results involving GPT-5/GPT-4.1/Gemini will also be hard to reproduce independently.

The theory relies on strong idealizations: discretized surprisal states are modeled as ergodic first-order Markov chains with bounded mixing and favorable stationary mass, and the discretization bound is existential rather than tightly linked to the practical k-means quantizer. The authors are honest that this is an approximation, but the theoretical guarantees should not be read as direct guarantees for natural text.

Some evaluation choices blur model selection and testing. The paper reports fixed k values but also uses k-optimized curves and an empirical constant for k scaling; it is not always clear whether k and thresholds are selected on held-out validation data, test data, or repeated test sweeps. This matters because several settings differ by only a few AUROC points.

The paper would benefit from deeper analysis of failure modes and fairness/ethics beyond the high-stakes warning. For AI-text detection, false positives can be socially costly; the manuscript gives low-FPR metrics but little discussion of variation across writing styles, non-native writers, demographic dialects, or benign human text edited by writing aids.

Presentation is mostly clear, but the manuscript is long and has some confusing or inconsistent statements and formatting issues. For example, the threshold-selection appendix says the GJS difference is positive when the test sequence is closer to the machine reference, whereas the earlier definition implies the opposite sign. Several tables are dense and hard to read.
